_comment: Budget gate for tools/run-slices.ps1. The driver reads this before EVERY slice, so editing
it takes effect immediately - no need to stop the driver.
TWO DIFFERENT JOBS, do not confuse them:
Slice caps are the rationing. They are what actually keeps the port to a defined share of
the allowance, and they are exact: the driver counts its own sessions.
Token caps are a circuit breaker, not a share. They exist to stop the driver on an
abnormally heavy day, and they are set well ABOVE typical usage on purpose.
The token figures are GLOBAL: every Claude Code session on this machine, and every token
type including cache reads, which dominate the total.
Calibrated 2026-08-29 from ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl. Typical usage on this machine is
about 2.9e9 tokens/day and 1.98e10/week by this metric. The caps below sit at roughly twice
the daily figure and 1.75x the weekly one. An earlier attempt to set them at HALF typical
usage was tested and rejected: the gate refused the very first slice, because an ordinary
working day passes that mark by the afternoon. A cap that never lets the driver start is not
a safeguard, it is a broken switch - so rationing lives in the slice caps and these numbers
only catch a runaway.
Recalibrate after Phase 1: docs/plan/slice-log.jsonl records what each slice actually cost,
which is the tokens-per-slice figure the design spec asks to be measured and recorded. Set
maxSlicesPerDay from that number and the share of allowance you want the port to have.
maxSlicesPerDay raised 3 -> 5 on 2026-08-30, by owner decision, against the first real
measurements: S06 completed on 48.6M tokens; S07 took two driver attempts, 54.5M and 46.9M,
both of which reached a green ratchet and then failed on the commit check. So a slice costs
roughly 50M tokens whether or not it lands, and the day S07 ran spent three slices of cap on
one slice of progress. Five leaves room for a slice to fail once and still be retried the
same day. NOTE the interaction with maxSlicesPerWeek, still 12: at five a day the weekly cap
now binds after two and a half busy days, which is the next number to revisit.
RECALIBRATED 2026-08-31 from Phase 2's measured figures, as the design spec asks. Eight
slices (S06-S13) cost about 12 driver-session equivalents - the log records 8, and undercounts:
S08's session died in a machine crash before it could log, and S07, S08 and S10 were each
finished by a follow-up session that never wrote a row. So budget ~1.5 sessions per slice, not
the 1.35 the roadmap recorded. A driver session averages 57M tokens; a completed one 55M and a
failed one 60M, because a slice fails late rather than early.
The slice caps are no longer pacing, and the honest reason is that they never were. Every
invocation in this workflow is `-MaxSlices 1`, which does one slice and exits, so no runaway
loop is reachable from the command anyone actually types. On 2026-08-30 the 5-a-day cap fired
three times and all three were false positives: legitimate work, lifted by hand each time.
What actually stopped work that night was the account's own limits - a session limit, then the
org monthly spend limit, which killed S10 mid-slice and which this file cannot see. Real
rationing lives in the Anthropic allowance; these numbers are here to stop a runaway
`-MaxSlices 50`, so they are set above any real day rather than at it.
maxSlicesPerDay 5 -> 10: the heaviest real day observed was 6 driver sessions in about twelve
hours. maxSlicesPerWeek 12 -> 30: Phase 3 is 13 slices and roughly 18 sessions, and at 12 it
could not finish inside a fortnight without a manual lift before nearly every slice.
The token caps are NOT raised. They are the circuit breaker that still works, they measure
global machine usage including cache reads, and they are correctly calibrated: the heaviest
day measured is 2.33e9 against a 6e9 cap, and the week sits at 1.98e10 against 3.5e10. Raising
a breaker until it cannot fire is how you end up with no breaker.
sliceTimeoutMinutes raised 120 -> 180 on 2026-08-30: a single `dotnet build` that APPEARED to
hang cost a slice about 12 minutes of its 120. The build itself was fine - the stall was in
the harness background-output mechanism returning empty - which is exactly why the ceiling
matters: the session cannot tell the two apart, and burns the clock either way. At that rate
a slice with a couple of stalls runs out of clock with the work nearly done and gets rolled
back.
maxSlicesPerDay 10 -> 20 on 2026-08-31, by owner decision, mid-Phase-3. The cap fired before
S16 with a true reading: the window is a rolling 24 hours, and S06-S13 from the previous day
plus S14 and S15 made exactly ten. The owner's answer was that the account allowance - the
thing that actually rations this work - had 85% of a five-hour session left, so the cap was
measuring the wrong quantity, which is what this file already says of the slice caps. Twenty
covers the rest of Phase 3 at ~1.5 sessions a slice without lifting it again mid-run.
maxSlicesPerWeek stays 30 and now binds first: ten are spent, so twenty remain. The token
caps are untouched and remain the circuit breaker that works.

maxSlicesPerDay 20 -> 30 and maxSlicesPerWeek 30 -> 60 on 2026-09-13, by owner decision: 33% of the weekly account allowance was unused with the renewal at 14:00 UK on 2026-09-14, and Phase 5 had spent 25 of the 30 weekly sessions in one day, so the weekly cap would have stopped Phase 6 after S45 with allowance to spare. The token caps are again untouched - they are the breaker that measures the machine rather than the plan.

maxSlicesPerWeek 60 -> 90 on 2026-09-16, by owner decision: S52 (oracle hardening) has run 18 sittings judging the seed sweep's divergence rows one family at a time, and the rolling-week count reached 60 at 01:32 UK with 22 of 37 rows still to judge and the rest of Phase 6 (S52b-S57) queued. The count would not have fallen below 60 until 2026-09-18. Tokens were at 8.66e9 of the 3.5e10 weekly breaker, which stays untouched.

sliceTimeoutMinutes 240 -> 285 on 2026-09-20: the owner asked for fewer restarts. Every fresh sitting spends 5M-10M tokens re-orienting, and 240 minutes forced a checkpoint inside almost every five-hour window; 285 lets one sitting span most of a window, with the allowance hook and the deadline line still ending it early when they must (spec amendment 34).

sliceTimeoutMinutes 180 -> 240 on 2026-09-13: S42 and S43 each ran a sitting to 165 minutes and S43's second sitting to the wire. Safe to raise now because the kill is no longer the only backstop - the session hook tells the session its remaining time from 30 minutes out, the driver keeps a green checkpoint commit on a failed sitting, and the heartbeat alarm follows the sitting's deadline.
